content.comment_body: Hello, I'm looking to find out how much electrical load (in watts) a [product_name] unit can handle. I'm considering installing 10 to 30 W LED flood lights in my garden, using the [product_name] as a timer and switch for these lights. Can the [product_name] safely support the wattage without the risk of overload, and is it possible to connect the LED flood lights directly to it? Thank you, [user_name]

Refer to the manual on page 236 ([article_no]). Key details: - Output type: Relay outputs - Electrical isolation: Yes - Organized in groups of 1 - Capable of digital input control - Max continuous current: 10 A per relay - Surge current (incandescent lamp load, 25000 operations): • At 230/240 V AC: max 30 A, 1000 W • At 115/120 V AC: max 30 A, 500 W - Fluorescent tube loads (25000 operations): • With ballast: 10 x 58 W (at 230/240 V AC) • Conventionally compensated: 1 x 58 W (at 230/240 V AC) • Uncompensated: 10 x 58 W (at 230/240 V AC) - Short circuit protection, cos 1: Power protection B16, 600A - Short circuit protection, cos 0.5–0.7: Power protection B16, 900A - No derating; operates across full temperature range - Parallel output circuits for increased power: Not permitted - Optional output relay protection: max 16 A, characteristic B16

analysis.insight_summary: The user is seeking guidance about the electrical load capacity of a [product_name] for a timer-operated garden lighting setup, specifically whether it can safely control and switch 10–30 W LED floodlights directly. Another user shares the relay output specifications from the manual, indicating current, voltage, and power limits, as well as circuit protection recommendations. Key UX takeaway: users need clear and easily accessible information about permissible load connections and hardware safety.
analysis.user_expectations: The user expects the [product_name] to reliably and safely operate LED flood lights directly, without causing overload or hardware failure.
